title: Error-detected surgery on Iceberg codes
authors: Andrea Di Fini, Samuel Crew, Laura Pecorari, Guido Pupillo
abstract: We construct explicit error-detecting surgery gadgets---small systems of auxiliary qubits and checks---for the high-rate Iceberg codes $[[2N,2N-2,2]]$, to perform fault-detected measurements of logical Pauli products. The construction follows the perspective of surgery as the gauging of a logical operator, regarded as a symmetry of the code. We give a complete classification of logical Pauli operators under the permutation automorphism group of the Iceberg code, reducing the construction to one gadget per orbit, and we verify with circuit-level simulations that the gadgets are fault-detecting, with the expected post-selected logical error rate. The gadgets require reconfigurable long-range connectivity, available on platforms such as neutral-atom arrays, making an error-detected demonstration of Pauli-based computation a natural near-term experiment. The paper doubles as a self-contained introduction to gauging and code surgery, developed alongside a simple worked example.
summary: This paper presents a method called 'code surgery' to perform measurements of logical Pauli operators in fault-tolerant quantum computation using Iceberg codes. By viewing measurement as gauging a global symmetry, the authors construct explicit gadgets that are proven to be fault-detecting via simulation. This makes it a highly relevant theoretical roadmap for building complex quantum computations on next-generation hardware.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a fault-tolerant method for measuring logical Pauli products within quantum error-correcting codes.
main_result: The authors successfully construct explicit, fault-detecting surgery gadgets for the high-rate Iceberg codes, showing that measurement can be achieved by gauging global symmetries of the code Hamiltonian.
method: The technique involves 'code surgery,' which treats logical measurements as gauging a global symmetry. This is formalized by adjoining auxiliary qubits to make the operator local, followed by a reverse deformation process.
model_or_system: The focus is on the Iceberg codes $	ext{[[2N, 2N-2, 2]]}$ and their associated Hamiltonians. The theoretical framework utilizes concepts from lattice gauge theory applied to quantum error correction.
key_observables: Fault detection requires suppressing the post-selected logical error rate by $O(p^2)$ relative to the physical error probability $p$. Key observables include the probability distribution $	ext{Pr}[\mu]$ of measurement outcomes.
important_parameters: The code parameters are $[[2N, 2N-2, 2]]$, and the construction depends on classifying logical Pauli operators into orbits under the permutation automorphism group $S_{2N}$.
main_assumptions: The gadgets require reconfigurable long-range connectivity for physical implementation. The analysis relies on mapping measurements to algebraic structures defined by boundary and cycle spaces over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the Pauli-based compilation of a GHZ gate using measurement sequences, while Figure 2 shows the physical layout structure for the Iceberg code.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the concept via a small warm-up example (four spins), then generalizes this to the Iceberg codes by classifying logical operators into orbits. It details the gauging procedure and concludes with circuit simulations confirming fault detection.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges abstract quantum error correction theory (gauging symmetries) with concrete, near-term physical implementations on platforms like neutral atoms that support long-range connectivity.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Pauli-based compilation of the four-qubit GHZ example. The Clifford circuit (a) compiles to the sequence of Pauli-product measurements (b), with outcomes (m0, . . . , m3) re- producing the readout bits up to a Pauli frame correction.
Figure 2: A physical layout of the [[2N, 2N −2, 2]] Iceberg code qubits.

Figure 3: The auxiliary graph Γ for the weight-four seed XXZZII of the [[6, 4, 2]] Iceberg code. The six data qubits are drawn as outward spokes of a hexagon, with the support of the seed labelled by Pauli type and the two unsupported qubits in grey. Gauge qubits live on the edges of Γ (blue and green): the path along the hexagon is closed into a four-cycle by a chord. Gauss-law checks Gv sit at the pink vertices and the flux check B on the enclosed face (red). The dressings of the two global checks are marked in green: WZ = sZ τ Z e0 (light green) and WX = sX τ Z e2 (dark green).

Figure 4: The panels depict the stabiliser structure of the merged [[4, 2, 2]] Iceberg code for different seed operators. The black circles represent the four physical data qubits, and the purple circles represent the gauge qubits. The green ancilla WX measures the X-type stabiliser, the black ancilla WZ measures the Z-type stabiliser, and the colored ancillas Gv0, Gv1 and Gv2 are the Gauss-law checks at each support vertex.
Figure 5: Post-selected logical error rate for the [[4, 2, 2]] (top) and [[6, 4, 2]] (bottom) seed gadgets, run A (left) and run B (right). Error bars are smaller than the marker size.
